selectedIdea.evidence:

selectedIdea.title: Small, explicit choices to reduce entry friction: Moorfield Choir’s newcomer-first setup and what it reveals
selectedIdea.description: Moorfield’s public notice and rehearsal practices show a deliberate, low-friction approach for hesitant adults (no auditions, no music-reading requirement, a listening option during a shared warm-up, a late-entry window, and a free first taster). Member responses from an October rehearsal single out “welcome” as the dominant reason people return, but the choir has not measured the effect of these choices. The story: community groups can design concrete, low-cost practices to make attendance easier and more imaginable — and should pair them with basic measurement to understand their impact.
selectedIdea.audience: Community choir leaders, volunteer arts organisers, local cultural participation coordinators.
selectedIdea.rationale: Why it matters: Many community groups struggle to attract tentative newcomers. The Moorfield example provides an evidence-grounded illustration of practical steps that explicitly lower social and logistical barriers and language that helps a hesitant person ‘picture the evening’. Reporting that members cite welcome most often gives this approach immediate relevance. It also highlights a common follow-on gap: operational choices are made without measurement, so their actual effect remains unknown. This idea is useful because it translates concrete, replicable practices into an agenda (design low-friction experiences + measure them) that other groups can apply.
selectedIdea.evidence: Explicit facts: the notice states there are “no auditions and no requirement to read music”; “the first twenty minutes are a shared warm-up; newcomers may listen before joining in”; session begins at 19:00 with quiet entry allowed until 19:20; “A first taster is free”; the notice is “intended to help a hesitant newcomer picture the evening and decide whether to come.” Member feedback: after the October rehearsal 12 of 19 answered a short question about returning; 8 mentioned the welcome, 3 mentioned the songs, and 1 mentioned both. Limitations/interpretation: the source does not measure attendance changes tied to these policies, nor does it report any pre/post confidence survey or comparison with a fixed-start rehearsal — so causal impact is unknown.

selectedIdea.title: What volunteer sighting counts at Alder Mere can — and can’t — tell us about reed-warbler numbers
selectedIdea.description: Use the autumn note to explain a single central point: raw sighting tallies (41 on the east boardwalk vs 18 on the west) are useful observations but, as recorded here, cannot be treated as direct measures of bird abundance without accounting for differing route coverage, times of day, and repeat detections.
selectedIdea.audience: Reserve staff, volunteer recorders, interested walkers and local conservation-minded readers.
selectedIdea.rationale: Why it matters: Readers who care about local wildlife often see simple counts and assume they indicate population differences. This piece would show how methodological details in the note (different visit frequencies, different hours, unequal distances, and the absence of a pre-cutting baseline) limit what the data can support, and why the reserve is rightly cautious about using the counts to justify habitat interventions. Gaps and uncertainty: The source does not provide route distances, detection effort per visit, whether sightings are repeat individuals, or statistical methods for adjusting counts — all of which would be needed to turn sightings into abundance estimates.
selectedIdea.evidence: Facts from the note: volunteers logged 41 reed-warbler sightings from the east route and 18 from the west; the east route was visited on six mornings, the west on three afternoons; observers used the same written recording sheet but worked at different hours and did not cover the same distance; counts are described as 'sightings, not identified individual birds'; the reserve team will compare route coverage before deciding whether the counts can inform habitat intervention.

selectedIdea.audience: Digital humanities project leads, archivists, UX designers for cultural heritage websites, multilingual content managers

Gaps & uncertainty: The evidence is limited (30 invites, 9 feedback-form opens, 4 comments) and no formal usability or comprehension testing was done, so the scale and specifics of the problem beyond initial reports are unknown.

selectedIdea.title: A small, generic editorial-rule change can flip the editorial hierarchy and derail an output pipeline
selectedIdea.description: Adding a single reusable instruction — “Preserve Editorial Intent from the Synthesis” — to the Narrative user prompt caused the pipeline to subordinate company identity and audience scope and to make orchestration the central message, producing consistently worse Narrative and Compose scores and a decision to rollback.
selectedIdea.audience: Prompt engineers, narrative designers, content ops and product communications leads responsible for AI-assisted content pipelines.
selectedIdea.rationale: This experiment provides direct evidence that even a short, generic editorial instruction can change model behaviour in a stable, repeatable way that matters for publishable output. Teams that modify narrative prompts need objective, task-specific validation (rubrics, multiple runs, gated criteria) because surface-preserving language alone can unintentionally reweight themes and introduce unsupported claims.
selectedIdea.evidence:
- Candidate prompt change: added section titled “Preserve Editorial Intent from the Synthesis.” (prompt-changes/Narrative.user.prompt.diff).  
- Only Narrative.user.prompt.txt changed; all other prompt files and inputs identical.  
- Narrative mean score: Baseline 6.00/10 vs Candidate 4.00/10.  
- Compose mean score: Baseline 5.67/10 vs Candidate 3.33/10.  
- Candidate runs uniformly lowered A (identity/audience) scores and failed C (theme hierarchy) — orchestration became central in all candidate runs.  
- Decision: Do not promote; production prompt restored byte-for-byte to baseline (restored SHA-256 matches baseline).

selectedIdea.evidence: Explicit cross-experiment finding: “Narrative is the most recurrent first visible hierarchy shift in the available records.” Examples: Experiment 007 candidate runs 001–002 show Synthesis preserved Nuëyon/Compose but Narrative turned it into an orchestration through-line; Experiment 009 baseline 002/003 and all three Candidate runs localize first hierarchy shifts at Narrative; Experiment 008 A-002 reports a first factual breach at Narrative. Important uncertainty: the source records intent only; the choir has not measured whether these features actually reduced hesitation, increased attendance, or improved retention.
